name: Azure App Service
summary: Azure’s platform for web apps and APIs: you rent a pool of VMs called an App Service plan, and every app you put in it runs on those VMs without you managing them.
intro: App Service runs web apps, REST APIs and mobile back ends written in .NET, Java (SE, Tomcat or JBoss), Node.js, Python or PHP, on Windows or Linux, or any app packaged as a custom container. Every app lives in an App Service plan, which fixes the region, the operating system, the pricing tier and the number and size of VM instances. You pay for the plan’s instances, not per app: all apps in a plan, plus their deployment slots, backups and WebJobs, share the same VMs and scale out together.

The tier sets what you get. Free and Shared run your app on VMs shared with other customers under a CPU quota and can’t scale out. Basic, Standard and the Premium tiers give the plan dedicated VMs (up to 3, 10 and 30 instances, the last on Premium v2 to v4), and IsolatedV2 runs them in an App Service Environment on a dedicated virtual network. From Standard up, deployment slots let you deploy to a live staging copy with its own hostname, warm it up, and swap it into production without dropping requests; swapping again rolls back.

Two features need no code. Built-in authentication, often called Easy Auth, signs users in through Microsoft Entra, Google, Facebook or X before requests reach your app. Scaling can be rule-based autoscale on CPU, memory or a schedule (Standard and up), or automatic scaling (Premium v2 to v4), where the platform adds instances as HTTP traffic grows and keeps prewarmed ones ready.
strengths: One plan can host many apps at no extra cost per app, and custom domains, SNI TLS certificates and deployment slots are free
Deployment slots (5 per app on Standard, 20 on Premium and Isolated) give zero-downtime releases and one-step rollback
Sign-in through Microsoft Entra, Google, Facebook or X with no SDK or code changes
Windows and Linux, code or containers, plus a Managed Instance option for legacy Windows apps that need COM, registry access or MSI installers
limits: On dedicated tiers you pay for every VM instance in the plan whether its apps are busy or idle; there is no scale to zero
Apps in one plan share the same VMs, so a busy app slows its neighbors; isolating an app means giving it its own plan
Free and Shared get 60 and 240 CPU minutes a day, run on VMs shared with other customers, and can’t scale out
Deployment slots and autoscale start at Standard, automatic scaling at Premium v2, and Basic stops at 3 instances

snippet.title: Deploy with the Azure CLI, then release through a staging slot
source: # Creates the plan and the app, then zip-deploys the current folder
az webapp deployment slot create --name shop-api \
# ...deploy the next release to the staging slot, test it, then:
az webapp deployment slot swap --name shop-api \

story: On June 7, 2012, Scott Guthrie announced Windows Azure Web Sites, a simpler way to deploy ASP.NET, Node.js and PHP sites that could “start small (and for free) and then scale up” as traffic grew. Up to 10 sites ran free in a shared, multi-tenant environment, and you could move them to a “reserved mode” where you were the only customer on the VM. Deploys came from FTP, Git, TFS or Web Deploy, and a new site was ready to deploy to in under 10 seconds.

Web Sites became generally available with an SLA on June 27, 2013, alongside new autoscale support. On March 24, 2015, Microsoft folded Azure Websites and Azure Mobile Services into a single product, Azure App Service, and added Logic Apps and API Apps. Web Apps kept all of Websites’ capabilities at the same price and was generally available from day one, while the other app types started in preview.

In September 2017 App Service became generally available on Linux too, with built-in images for ASP.NET Core, Node.js, PHP and Ruby, together with Web App for Containers, which deploys your own Docker image.

choices.choice: A free shared tier with a paid reserved tier above it
choices.why: Guthrie pitched Web Sites as a way to start a project at no cost on shared servers, then move to dedicated VMs and add instances as traffic grew, with the same deployment options at every size.

choices.choice: Pay for the VMs, not per app
choices.why: With App Service, Guthrie wrote, you could create any number of web, mobile, logic and API apps and run them on one App Service deployment at no additional cost. The plan is still the unit you pay for.

choices.choice: Deploy the way developers already worked
choices.why: From the start Web Sites accepted FTP, Git, TFS and Web Deploy, and Visual Studio and WebMatrix could publish directly, so existing ASP.NET and PHP teams could keep the tools they had.

timeline.text: Windows Azure Web Sites announced on June 7 for ASP.NET, Node.js and PHP
Web Sites generally available with an SLA, plus autoscale
Websites and Mobile Services merge into Azure App Service on March 24
App Service on Linux and Web App for Containers generally available
